prompt: What is the difference between expiration and eviction?

options.text: Expiration drops entries past their TTL; eviction drops entries to free room when memory is full
They are two names for the same mechanism: removing entries once the cache runs out of room
Expiration happens only when the cache is full; eviction happens on a timer per entry
Eviction removes entries that are wrong or stale; expiration removes the most popular ones

explanation: Expiration is about freshness and happens on a timer; eviction is about capacity and happens under memory pressure. (b) conflates them. (c) swaps them: running out of room triggers eviction, and the timer is expiration. (d) Neither mechanism knows whether an entry is wrong, and no sane policy targets popular entries.

prompt: Under LRU, which key is evicted when E is inserted?
scenario: An LRU cache holds 3 entries. It receives the requests A, B, C, B, A, then E.

options.text: A
B
C
E is rejected

explanation: After A, B, C, B, A the recency order (oldest first) is C, B, A, so C is least recently used. (a) A was just used. (b) B was used after C. (d) LRU always admits the new entry and evicts the victim.

prompt: What most likely caused the morning's low hit ratio?
scenario: A product cache uses plain LRU and runs at 97% hits all day. Every night at 02:00 a reconciliation job reads every one of 4 million products once through the same cache. Each morning the hit ratio starts near 40% and takes an hour to recover.

options.text: The job's one-off reads became the most recent entries and pushed out the hot set
The TTLs are too long, so the cache is full of stale products by each morning
The cache node restarts every night after the job and comes back empty each morning
LRU evicts the most recently used keys first, so the hot daytime set goes first

explanation: A scan makes millions of keys 'recent', pushing out the hot ones (cache pollution); morning traffic then misses until they reload. Fix it by routing the job around the cache or using a scan-resistant policy such as LFU. (b) Long TTLs would raise the hit ratio, not lower it. (c) Nothing suggests a restart, and the timing matches the job. (d) LRU evicts the least recently used.

prompt: Why does an O(1) LRU cache use a doubly linked list rather than a singly linked list?

options.text: To unlink a node in O(1), you need a pointer to its previous node
Doubly linked lists use less memory per node than singly linked ones
So the list can stay sorted by key, which makes lookups by key faster
Singly linked lists can't store a key and a value together in each node

explanation: Moving a hit entry to the front means unlinking it from the middle, which needs its predecessor; a singly linked list would need an O(n) walk. (b) They use more memory: one extra pointer per node. (c) LRU orders by recency, not key, and lookups go through the hash map. (d) is simply false: any node can hold a key and a value.

prompt: In the hash map + doubly linked list LRU, which operations are O(1)? (Choose all that apply.)

options.text: Looking up a key
Moving a hit entry to the most-recent end
Finding and removing the least recently used entry
Listing all keys in recency order

explanation: (a) is a hash map lookup. (b) is a constant number of pointer changes. (c) The victim is always the node next to the tail sentinel. (d) is O(n) because it must visit every node.

prompt: Why does a shared in-process LRU cache become a bottleneck on a many-core server?

options.text: Every get reorders the list, so even reads need exclusive access to shared state
Hash maps can't be read concurrently by design, so every lookup takes a global lock
LRU caches must write each hit to disk to persist recency, so reads queue on I/O
The capacity is split by the number of cores, so each core's share keeps missing

explanation: Reads mutate recency order, so they contend on a lock; libraries shard the cache or batch access updates. (b) Concurrent hash map reads are routine. (c) In-memory caches don't touch disk on hits. (d) Capacity doesn't depend on core count.

prompt: What is the problem with this LFU cache?
scenario: A video site's cache uses pure LFU with no decay. Last month's viral video, with 40 million hits, is still cached. Today's trending videos, each with a few thousand hits, keep getting evicted and reloaded.

options.text: Without decay, old counts never fade, so stale favourites crowd out what's popular now
LFU always evicts the most popular entry first, so trending videos are pushed out
The cache is actually using LRU by mistake, which keeps the oldest entries longest
The viral video's TTL is too short, so it keeps being reloaded ahead of new ones

explanation: Pure LFU remembers all history; decaying counts (as Redis's LFU mode does) lets past popularity fade. (b) LFU evicts the least frequently used. (c) LRU evicts the oldest-used entries first, so the old video would have been evicted long ago. (d) A short TTL would have removed the old video, which is the opposite of what's happening.

prompt: Which is a real advantage of FIFO eviction over LRU?

options.text: It never evicts hot keys, since they keep getting re-inserted on access
It does no bookkeeping on hits, so reads don't contend on shared state
It always achieves a higher hit ratio, since it keeps entries in order
It doesn't need a capacity limit, since old entries simply fall off

explanation: FIFO only acts on insert and evict, so hits are cheap and concurrent. (a) A hit doesn't re-insert anything, so FIFO can evict hot keys just because they're old. (c) Plain FIFO usually hits less than LRU; only some FIFO-based variants compete. (d) Entries only 'fall off' because of a capacity limit; every eviction policy exists because of one.

scenario: A team starts a fresh Redis instance, sets `maxmemory 4gb`, and uses it as a cache with a 1-hour TTL on every key. Under peak load, writes start failing with out-of-memory errors while reads keep working.

options.text: The default policy is noeviction, so Redis rejects writes once full instead of evicting
Setting a TTL on every key disables eviction, so Redis can only wait for expiry
Redis can't store more than 4 GB per instance, so writes past that point fail
The keys are too large to evict, so Redis refuses new writes until some expire

explanation: With noeviction, hitting maxmemory makes memory-needing writes fail. More than 4 GB was written within one TTL period, so expiry alone couldn't keep up. Set allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu. (b) TTLs make keys eligible for volatile-* policies; they don't disable eviction. (c) 4 GB is the configured limit, not a Redis maximum. (d) Key size doesn't block eviction.

prompt: Which policy lets the cache entries be evicted while protecting the sessions?
scenario: One Redis instance holds user sessions, which must never be evicted, and cached page fragments, which can be. Memory is nearly full.

options.text: allkeys-lru, with no TTLs anywhere, so the least-used keys go first
volatile-lru, with TTLs set on page fragments and no TTL on sessions
noeviction, so nothing is ever removed and the sessions stay safe
allkeys-random, so sessions and fragments are evicted at an equal rate

explanation: volatile-* policies only evict keys that have a TTL, so fragments with TTLs are candidates and sessions without TTLs aren't. Separate instances would be cleaner still. (a) and (d) could evict sessions. (c) would make writes fail instead of evicting fragments.

options.text: It keeps a full doubly linked list across all keys, like a textbook LRU cache
It samples a few keys (maxmemory-samples, default 5) and evicts the one idle longest
It evicts keys in key-name order, starting from the lowest hash slot number
It evicts the largest keys first, since they free the most memory per eviction

explanation: Redis samples a few keys using a per-key access stamp, evicts the one idle longest, and keeps a pool of good candidates between rounds; this avoids per-key list pointers. (a) is exactly what Redis avoids to save memory. (c) and (d) aren't Redis policies.
